title: Contrasting Agile, CI/CD, and Waterfall
html:
The Waterfall Model: One Direction, One Chance

The Waterfall model is the most traditional approach to software development. It organizes work into a fixed sequence of phases, where each phase must be fully completed before the next one begins — much like water flowing over a series of steps.
🎨 Nền ô:
Phase
What Happens
RequirementsAll business needs are documented upfront
System DesignArchitects create the technical blueprint
ImplementationDevelopers write the code
TestingQA tests the completed product
DeploymentThe product is released to users
MaintenanceBugs are fixed post-release

The Waterfall model works well when requirements are clearly defined, unlikely to change, and the project has a fixed scope and deadline — such as government contracts or compliance-driven systems.

However, its biggest weakness is inflexibility. If a requirement changes midway through the project, or a design flaw is discovered during testing, the team must loop all the way back to an earlier phase. This is costly, time-consuming, and disruptive.

For QA professionals, the Waterfall model means testing happens late — often under significant time pressure, with little opportunity to influence quality earlier in the process.

The Agile Model: Iterative, Collaborative, and Adaptive

Agile was created as a direct response to the rigidity of Waterfall. Rather than planning everything upfront and delivering one large product at the end, Agile breaks work into short, repeating cycles called sprints — typically lasting one to four weeks.

At the end of each sprint, the team delivers a working, tested piece of software. Feedback is gathered, priorities are adjusted, and the next sprint begins. This cycle continues until the product is complete.

Key characteristics of Agile include:

  • Sprints: Short, time-boxed development cycles that produce a working product increment

  • Cross-functional teams: Developers, testers, designers, and business stakeholders collaborate daily

  • Continuous feedback: Requirements can evolve based on stakeholder input between sprints

  • Early and frequent testing: QA is embedded within each sprint, not saved for the end

For some professionals, Agile is a significant shift. You are no longer a gatekeeper at the end of the pipeline. You are an active collaborator throughout every sprint, writing test cases alongside developers, flagging issues early, and contributing to the team's shared definition of "done."

Don't worry if Agile feels like a lot to absorb at once. The key idea is simple: instead of one big release at the end, Agile delivers small, tested pieces of working software continuously throughout the project.

CI/CD: When Agile Meets Automation

Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) takes the Agile philosophy of frequent delivery and accelerates it dramatically through automation. While Agile teams might release working software at the end of each sprint, CI/CD teams can release updates multiple times per day.

CI/CD is not a replacement for Agile — it is an evolution of it, powered by automated tools and pipelines.

Here is how the two components work:

Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of developers merging their code changes into a shared repository frequently — sometimes multiple times per day. Each merge automatically triggers a build and a suite of automated tests. If a test fails, the team is alerted immediately, and the issue is fixed before it compounds.

Continuous Deployment (CD) takes the validated code from the CI process and automatically deploys it to a staging or production environment. This means that once code passes all automated checks, it can reach end-users within minutes, without manual intervention.

The Role of Automation in CI/CD

CI/CD pipelines depend entirely on test automation. Without automated tests running at every stage of the pipeline, the speed of CI/CD would be impossible to maintain safely. Manual testing simply cannot keep pace with code that changes multiple times a day.

Common types of automated tests in a CI/CD pipeline include:

  • Unit tests that verify individual components work in isolation

  • Integration tests that confirm different modules communicate correctly

  • Regression tests that ensure new changes haven't broken existing functionality

  • Smoke tests that quickly validate the most critical functions of the application after each deployment

For QA professionals, CI/CD means your role evolves further. Writing and maintaining automated test scripts becomes a core responsibility. You shift from manually executing test cases to designing and monitoring the automated safety net that protects every release.
